B738.name: Boeing 737-800
B738.notes: The workhorse of US domestic flying. Over 5,000 built. Its blended winglets, the upturned wingtips, cut fuel burn by about 4 percent.

B38M.name: Boeing 737 MAX 8
B38M.notes: The newest 737, with much larger engines and split-scimitar winglets. The engines are so big they had to be mounted higher and further forward on the wing.

B739.name: Boeing 737-900ER
B739.notes: The longest 737, stretched to carry up to 220 people.

B39M.name: Boeing 737 MAX 9
B39M.notes: A stretched MAX with up to 220 seats.

B737.name: Boeing 737-700
B737.notes: The smallest common 737 variant, a favourite of Southwest Airlines.

A319.name: Airbus A319
A319.engines: Two CFM56 or IAE V2500 turbofans
A319.notes: The short version of the A320 family. Airbus fly-by-wire: the pilots' sidesticks send electronic commands rather than moving cables.

A320.name: Airbus A320
A320.engines: Two CFM56 or IAE V2500 turbofans
A320.notes: The first airliner with digital fly-by-wire controls, introduced in 1988. Its wingtip fences or sharklets reduce drag.

A20N.name: Airbus A320neo
A20N.engines: Two Pratt & Whitney PW1100G or CFM LEAP-1A turbofans
A20N.notes: The neo (new engine option) burns about 15 percent less fuel than the original A320 thanks to huge new engines and sharklet wingtips.

A321.name: Airbus A321
A321.engines: Two CFM56 or IAE V2500 turbofans
A321.notes: The stretched A320, carrying up to 240 people.

A21N.name: Airbus A321neo
A21N.engines: Two PW1100G or CFM LEAP-1A turbofans
A21N.notes: Long-range single-aisle jet that now flies transatlantic routes once reserved for widebodies.

B752.name: Boeing 757-200
B752.engines: Two Rolls-Royce RB211 or Pratt & Whitney PW2000 turbofans
B752.notes: Famously overpowered for its size, with a steep climb; pilots call it the 'Atari Ferrari'. Out of production since 2004.

B763.name: Boeing 767-300
B763.engines: Two GE CF6, PW4000 or RB211 turbofans
B763.notes: A twin-aisle widebody with a 2-3-2 cabin, so most seats are a window or an aisle.

B788.name: Boeing 787-8 Dreamliner
B788.engines: Two GEnx or Rolls-Royce Trent 1000 turbofans
B788.notes: Half carbon-fibre composite by weight, with the largest windows of any airliner and cabin pressure set to a lower 1,800 m equivalent, which makes you feel better on arrival.

B789.name: Boeing 787-9 Dreamliner
B789.engines: Two GEnx or Rolls-Royce Trent 1000 turbofans
B789.notes: The stretched Dreamliner. Watch the wings: they flex upward by several metres in flight, by design.

B772.name: Boeing 777-200
B772.engines: Two GE90, PW4000 or Trent 800 turbofans
B772.notes: The first Boeing designed entirely on computers. Its GE90 engines are as wide as a 737 fuselage.

B77W.name: Boeing 777-300ER
B77W.notes: The most powerful jet engines ever flown hang under this wing, each producing over 115,000 pounds of thrust.

A332.name: Airbus A330-200
A332.engines: Two GE CF6, PW4000 or Trent 700 turbofans
A332.notes: A long-range widebody with a 2-4-2 economy cabin.

A333.name: Airbus A330-300
A333.engines: Two GE CF6, PW4000 or Trent 700 turbofans
A333.notes: Stretched A330, common on transatlantic and Hawaii routes.

A359.name: Airbus A350-900
A359.notes: Carbon-fibre fuselage and wings, with curved wingtips and the quietest cabin of any widebody.

E170.name: Embraer E170
E170.notes: A regional jet with a 2-2 cabin: every seat is a window or an aisle.

E175.name: Embraer E175
E175.notes: The most common regional jet in the United States, flown by partner airlines for the majors. Every seat is a window or an aisle.

E75L.name: Embraer E175 (long wing)
E75L.notes: The E175 with larger winglets for better fuel economy.

E190.name: Embraer E190
E190.notes: A 100-seat regional jet with a 2-2 cabin.

CRJ9.name: Bombardier CRJ900
CRJ9.notes: A stretched regional jet with rear-mounted engines, so the wing view is uninterrupted.

CRJ7.name: Bombardier CRJ700
CRJ7.notes: A 70-seat regional jet with rear-mounted engines.

DH8D.name: De Havilland Dash 8-400
DH8D.engines: Two Pratt & Whitney Canada PW150 turboprops
DH8D.notes: A fast turboprop that cruises lower than jets, which means a closer, more detailed view of the ground.

AT76.name: ATR 72-600
AT76.notes: A short-haul turboprop; low and slow is good for sightseeing.

BCS3.name: Airbus A220-300
BCS3.notes: Designed by Bombardier as the C Series. Its 2-3 cabin means fewer middle seats, and its windows are unusually large.

BCS1.name: Airbus A220-100
BCS1.notes: The smaller A220 with a 2-3 cabin and big windows.
